{{short description|Longest side of a right-angled triangle, the side opposite of the right angle}}
[[File:Hypotenuse.svg|thumb|right|A right-angled triangle and its hypotenuse]]

In [[geometry]], a '''hypotenuse''' is the side of a [[right triangle]] that is opposite to the [[right angle]].<ref>{{Cite EB1911 |wstitle= Triangle (geometry) |volume= 27 |page= 258|quote=...Also a right-angled triangle has one angle a right angle, the side opposite this angle being called the hypotenuse;...|short=1}}</ref> It is always the longest side of the triangle. The other two sides of a right triangle are called [[cathetus|legs]] or catheti.<ref name="africk">{{cite book |last=Africk |first=Henry |year=2021 |title=Elementary College Geometry |edition=2021 |publisher=New York City College of Technology |url=https://academicworks.cuny.edu/ny_oers/44/ }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Cathetus |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Cathetus.html |website=MathWorld |publisher=Wolfram Research |access-date=2025-12-17}}</ref>

The [[length]] of the hypotenuse can be found using the [[Pythagorean theorem]], which states that the [[Square (algebra)|square]] of the length of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides. As an algebraic formula, this can be written as <math>a^2 + b^2 = c^2</math>, where {{tmath|a}} is the length of one leg, {{tmath|b}} is the length of the other leg, and {{tmath|c}} is the length of the hypotenuse.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Moland Jr |first=Jesse |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dWAXwWpQa5EC&q=hypotenuse |title=I Hate Trig!: A Practical Guide to Understanding Trigonometry |date=August 2009 |publisher=Jesse Moland |isbn=978-1-4486-4707-1 |pages=1 |language=en}}</ref> For example, if the two legs of a right triangle have lengths 3 and 4, respectively, then the hypotenuse has length 5, because {{tmath|1=\textstyle 3^2 + 4^2 = 25 = 5^2}}.<ref name="africk"/>

==Etymology==
{{wiktionary|ὑποτείνουσα}}
The English word ''hypotenuse'' is derived from the {{langx|grc|ὑποτείνουσα|hypoteinousa|stretching under}}. It refers to how the hypotenuse "stretches under" the right angle.<ref name="etymonline">{{cite web |url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/hypotenuse |title=hypotenuse |website=Online Etymology Dictionary |language=en |access-date=2019-05-14}}</ref><ref name="collins">{{cite web |url=https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/hypotenuse |title=hypotenuse definition and word origin |website=Collins Dictionary |publisher=Collins |access-date=2022-04-12}}</ref>

It was [[loanword|loaned]] into [[Late Latin|Latin]] as {{lang|la|hypotenusa}} and later into [[French language|French]] as {{lang|fr|hypoténuse}}.<ref name="cnrtl">{{cite web |url=http://www.cnrtl.fr/etymologie/hypotenuse |title=Hypotenuse |website=CNRTL |language=fr |access-date=2025-12-17}}</ref> It first appeared in English in the 1570s.<ref name="etymonline" />

The equivalent Latin verb, {{langlink|la|subtended angle|subtend}}, is still used in English in a more general sense to refer to any line or curve stretched across an angle.

==Properties==
{{anchor|Calculating the hypotenuse}}
===Pythagorean theorem===
[[File:Pythagorean.svg|thumb|alt=A right triangle with a square attached to each edge|An illustration of the Pythagorean theorem]]
{{main article|Pythagorean theorem}}
The [[Pythagorean theorem]] states that the [[square (algebra)|square]] of the length of the hypotenuse ({{tmath|c}}) is equal to the [[sum (mathematics)|sum]] of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides ({{tmath|a}} and {{tmath|b}}). This can be written as the [[equation]] {{tmath|1=a^2 + b^2 = c^2}}. To calculate the length of the hypotenuse, the equation can be rearranged to solve for {{tmath|c}} by taking the [[square root]] of both sides, yielding {{tmath|1= c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} }}. This is sometimes known as [[Pythagorean addition]].<ref name="moler-morrison-ibm">{{cite journal | last1 = Moler | first1 = Cleve | author1-link = Cleve Moler | last2 = Morrison | first2 = Donald | citeseerx = 10.1.1.90.5651 | doi = 10.1147/rd.276.0577 | issue = 6 | journal = IBM Journal of Research and Development | pages = 577–581 | title = Replacing square roots by Pythagorean sums | url = https://scholar.archive.org/work/vn5a4l3fhfbkzomjj4dypacw7q | volume = 27 | year = 1983}}</ref> For example, if the two legs of a right triangle have lengths 3 and 4, respectively, then the hypotenuse has length 5, because {{tmath|1=\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5}}.<ref name="africk"/>

The Pythagorean theorem is a special case of the [[law of cosines]], a more general theorem relating the lengths of sides in any triangle. It states that {{tmath|1=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos{\theta}=c^2}} where {{tmath|\theta}} is the angle between sides {{tmath|a}} and {{tmath|b}}.<ref name="leff">{{cite book |title=PreCalculus the Easy Way |last=Leff |first=Lawrence S. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=y_7yrqrHTb4C&pg=PA326 |page=326 |isbn=0-7641-2892-2 |publisher=Barron's Educational Series |date=2005-05-01}}</ref> When {{tmath|\theta}} is {{tmath|\tfrac{\pi}{2} }} radians or 90°, then {{tmath|1=\cos{\theta} = 0}} and the formula reduces to the usual Pythagorean theorem.

===Sine and cosine===
[[File:Trigono sine en2.svg|thumb|upright=1|For the angle {{math|1=''α''}}, the sine function gives the ratio of the length of the opposite side to the length of the hypotenuse]]
{{main article|Sine and cosine}}
The [[sine and cosine]] functions (sin and cos) describe the relationship of the hypotenuse to the lengths and angles of the other two sides. These, along with [[tangent function|tangent]] (tan), are the most common [[trigonometric functions]].<ref name="africk" />

The trig functions are usually described in terms of one of the [[acute angles]] of a right triangle ({{tmath|\angle A}}), the [[cathetus|leg]] that is adjacent to that angle, and the leg that is opposite that angle. The sine of the acute angle gives the ratio of the opposite leg to the hypotenuse, while the cosine of the angle gives the ratio of the adjacent leg to the hypotenuse. This can be written as the [[equations]]:
<math display="block">
 \sin(\angle A) = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad
 \cos(\angle A) = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}.
</math>

The definitions of the sine, cosine and tangent functions are often remembered using the [[mnemonic]] "[[SOH-CAH-TOA]]", where "SOH" stands for "sine = opposite / hypotenuse", "CAH" stands for "cosine = adjacent / hypotenuse", and "TOA" stands for "tangent = opposite / adjacent".<ref name="africk" />

==In computer programming==
Many [[programming languages]] support a version of the [[ISO C]] standard function <code>hypot(x, y)</code>, which calculates the hypotenuse of a right triangle using the [[Pythagorean theorem]].<ref>{{cite web |title=hypot(3) |url=https://manpages.debian.org/bullseye/manpages-dev/hypot.3.en.html |work=Linux Programmer's Manual |access-date=4 December 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Ivor Horton's Beginning Java 2|first=Ivor|last=Horton|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|year=2005|isbn=9780764568749|page=57|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=h0Uhz4lBoF8C&pg=PA57}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Learning Scientific Programming with Python|first=Christian|last=Hill|edition=2nd|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2020|isbn=9781108787468|page=14|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XAIHEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA14}}</ref> The function is designed not to fail where the straightforward calculation might [[arithmetic overflow|overflow]] or [[arithmetic underflow|underflow]]. It can often be more accurate and slower than the straightforward calculation.<ref name="moler-morrison-ibm" />

Some languages have extended the definition to higher dimensions.  For example, [[C++17]] supports <code>std::hypot(x, y, z)</code> which gives the length of the diagonal of a [[rectangular cuboid]] with edge lengths ''x'', ''y'', and ''z''.<ref>{{cite web |title=C++ std::hypot |url=https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/numeric/math/hypot |work=C++ Language Manual |access-date=6 June 2024}}</ref> [[Python language|Python]] 3.8 includes a version of <code>math.hypot</code> which can handle an arbitrary number of arguments.<ref>{{cite web |title=Python math.hypot |url=https://docs.python.org/3/library/math.html |work=Python Language Manual |access-date=6 June 2024}}</ref>
